chapterNote: The last of the great Solomonic collections circles back to its dearest themes: discipline that saves and the stiff neck that destroys (v.1), and above all the difference a ruler makes — when the righteous hold sway the people sing, when the wicked govern the people groan (vv.2, 4, 12, 16, 26). Threaded through the public concern for justice runs the private work of the home: the rod and reproof that give a child wisdom, the son corrected who becomes a father's rest (vv.15, 17, 21). The chapter ends where the book began, in two grand contrasts — the fear of man that snares against the trust in the LORD that lifts to safety (v.25), and the mutual loathing of the just and the wicked, who can no more abide each other than light and dark (v.27).

1.text: A man who, after much reproof, only stiffens his neck will be shattered in an instant — and beyond all healing.
1.amp: A man [ish] who, after being often reproved [tokachat — rebuke meant to correct], hardens [qashah — makes stubborn, sets like stone] his neck [oreph — the nape, the stiffened back of the neck] will suddenly be broken [shavar — shattered, snapped] — and there is no remedy [marpeh — healing, cure].
1.notes: qashah (H7185) is to make hard or obstinate; the 'stiff neck' (oreph, H6203) is Israel's classic posture of rebellion (Ex 32:9). The terror of the verse is its suddenness: repeated mercy spurned ends in shavar (H7665), a break too late for any marpeh (H4832) to mend.

2.text: When the righteous grow many and great, the people rejoice; but when a wicked man rules, the people groan.
2.amp: When the righteous [tsaddiq] increase and grow great [rabah — multiply, become many], the people [am] rejoice [samach — are glad]; but when the wicked [rasha] bears rule [mashal — governs, has dominion], the people [am] groan [anach — sigh and moan under the weight].
2.notes: anach (H584) is the heavy sigh of those pressed down by oppression (cf. Ex 2:23). The verse states the book's political conviction: government is never neutral — the moral character of those in power becomes the daily atmosphere the common am (H5971) must breathe.

3.text: A man who loves wisdom brings joy to his father, but a companion of harlots squanders his wealth.
3.amp: A man [ish] who loves [ahab — desires, delights in] wisdom [chokmah] gladdens [samach] his father [ab]; but one who keeps company [raah — shepherds, befriends, runs with] with harlots [zanah — those who play the prostitute] destroys [abad — causes to perish] his substance [hon — wealth, riches].
3.notes: the verse plays on raah (H7462), to shepherd or befriend — the loving son tends wisdom, the lost son tends harlots, and what he 'shepherds' devours him. hon (H1952), the wealth abad (H6) consumes, recalls the prodigal pattern (Lk 15:13); folly is not only sin but ruinous economics.

4.text: By justice a king gives his land a firm foundation, but a man greedy for bribes tears it down.
4.amp: By justice [mishpat — right judgment, fair ruling] a king establishes [amad — makes stand firm, gives stability to] the land [eretz]; but a man [ish] of forced gifts [terumah — here, the bribe extracted as a 'contribution'] tears it down [haras — demolishes, pulls to the ground].
4.notes: amad (H5975) and haras (H2040) are opposites — to make stand and to pull down. A throne built on mishpat (H4941) steadies a whole eretz (H776); a ruler who treats office as a means to terumah (H8641), payments squeezed from the people, demolishes the very ground he stands on.

5.text: A man who flatters his neighbor is spreading a net for his own feet.
5.amp: A man [geber] who flatters [chalaq — makes his words smooth and slippery] his neighbor [rea — friend, companion] is spreading [paras — stretching out] a net [resheth] for his feet [paam — his steps].
5.notes: chalaq (H2505) is to make smooth — the same slick speech the seductress uses in 2:16. Flattery is dressed as friendship but works as a snare; the one who spreads it may mean to trip his neighbor, but the proverb leaves it open whose paam (H6471) the net finally catches.

6.text: An evil man is trapped in the snare of his own sin, but the righteous runs ahead singing and glad.
6.amp: In the transgression [pesha — rebellion, breach of trust] of an evil [ra] man [ish] there is a snare [moqesh — a trap with its bait]; but the righteous [tsaddiq] sings out [ranan — shouts aloud for joy] and is glad [sameach].
6.notes: moqesh (H4170) is a fowler's trap — the evil man's own pesha (H6588) closes on him like a baited spring. Set against his entanglement is the tsaddiq (H6662), unbound and ranan (H7442), free to sing; sin shackles, righteousness liberates.

7.text: The righteous takes up the cause of the poor; the wicked has no mind even to understand it.
7.amp: The righteous [tsaddiq] takes account of [yada — knows, gives attention to] the legal cause [din — the plea, the case at law] of the poor [dal — the weak, the lowly]; but the wicked [rasha] does not discern [biyn] enough to know [daat] it.
7.notes: yada (H3045), to know, here means to care about and act upon. The tsaddiq enters into the din (H1779), the courtroom plea, of the dal (H1800); the rasha lacks the very daat (H1847) — the moral knowledge — to perceive that the poor have a case at all. Indifference is its own kind of injustice.

8.text: Scoffers set a city ablaze, but the wise turn back wrath.
8.amp: Scornful [latson — mocking, derisive] men [enosh] inflame [puach — blow upon, set ablaze] a city [qiryah]; but the wise [chakam] turn back [shub — cause to return, reverse] wrath [aph — the hot anger, literally the flaring nostril].
8.notes: the margin offers 'set a city on fire' — mockers blow on its passions like a man fanning coals until the whole qiryah (H7151) is in flames. The chakam (H2450) does the opposite work, causing aph (H639), kindled anger, to shub (H7725) and die down. A city's peace hangs on which kind of speaker it heeds.

9.text: When a wise man takes a fool to court, the fool only rages or laughs, and there is no settling it.
9.amp: If a wise [chakam] man [ish] goes to law [shaphat — contends, pleads a case] with a foolish [evil — thick-headed, morally senseless] man [ish], the fool rages [ragaz — storms, quakes with fury] or laughs [sachaq — jeers and mocks], and there is no rest [nachat — no quiet, no resolution].
9.notes: shaphat (H8199) here is to argue a case before the judges. The futility is in the fool's two moods — ragaz (H7264), explosive anger, and sachaq (H7832), dismissive laughter — both of which refuse the very thing a hearing is for. With the evil (H191) there is no nachat (H5183), no coming to terms; reason cannot land where it is not received.

10.text: Bloodthirsty men hate the blameless, but the upright seek to guard his life.
10.amp: Men [enosh] of blood [dam — bloodshed] hate [sane — are hostile to] the blameless man [tam — the one of whole, undivided integrity]; but the upright [yashar] seek [baqash] his life [nephesh — his very being].
10.notes: the contrast turns on what each party seeks of the tam (H8535): the 'men of blood' (the Hebrew is literally that, dam, H1818) hate him with murderous intent, while the yashar (H3477) baqash (H1245) his nephesh (H5315) — seek it to protect, not to destroy. Integrity itself provokes the violent and draws the loyal.

11.text: A fool lets out his whole temper, but a wise man holds it back and stills it within.
11.amp: A fool [kesil] sends out [yatsa — lets pour forth] all his spirit [ruach — here, his temper, the gust of his anger]; but a wise [chakam] man stills [shabach — hushes, holds back] it until afterward [achor — keeping it behind him].
11.notes: ruach (H7307), breath or wind, stands for the surge of feeling the kesil (H3684) vents unchecked. shabach (H7623) can mean to soothe a storm to calm (Ps 65:7); the chakam masters his ruach the way one stills rough water, holding it achor (H268), behind and under control, rather than spending it all at once.

12.text: If a ruler gives ear to lies, all his officials turn wicked.
12.amp: If a ruler [mashal — one who governs] gives heed [qashab — listens intently] to a word [dabar] of falsehood [sheqer — deception, a lie], all his servants [sharath — his attending officials] become wicked [rasha].
12.notes: qashab (H7181) is the leaning-in listening Wisdom asked for in 2:2 — here bent toward sheqer (H8267). A court takes the moral shape of its head: when the one who rules rewards the lie, every sharath (H8334) who would serve him learns that wickedness is the way to be heard. Corruption flows down from the throne.

13.text: Set the destitute beside the man who preys on him, and one thing binds them together — it is the LORD who kindles light in the eyes of both alike.
13.amp: The poor man [rush — the destitute] and the man [ish] of oppressions [tok — the one who deceives and extorts] meet together; the LORD [YHWH] gives light [or — makes shine] to the eyes [ayin] of both [shenayim].
13.notes: or (H215) of the eyes is the gift of life itself — to have light in the ayin (H5869) is to be alive and seeing (cf. 1 Sam 14:27). The crushing rush (H7326) and his crusher share one Maker, who sustains the breath of each; the verse is a quiet warning that the oppressor lives only by the mercy of the God who also sees the oppressed.

14.text: A king who judges the poor with faithfulness — his throne will stand firm forever.
14.amp: The king who judges [shaphat] the poor [dal] in faithfulness [emeth — truth, reliable steadiness], his throne [kisse] shall be established [kun — made firm and lasting] forever [ad — in perpetuity].
14.notes: emeth (H571) is truth as faithfulness — judgment that can be relied on because it does not bend to wealth. The reward is dynastic permanence: a kisse (H3678) kun (H3559) ad (H5703), a throne made firm into perpetuity. The way to lasting power is the very justice toward the dal (H1800) that the powerful are tempted to neglect.

15.text: The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself shames his mother.
15.amp: The rod [shebet — the staff of correction] and reproof [tokachat — corrective rebuke] give [natan] wisdom [chokmah]; but a boy [naar — a youth, a lad] left to himself [shalach — sent off, let go unchecked] brings his mother [em] to shame [bosh — public disgrace].
15.notes: shebet (H7626), the rod, and tokachat (H8433), the spoken rebuke, work as a pair — discipline of hand and of word together natan (H5414) chokmah. The danger is not harsh correction but no correction: the naar (H5288) shalach (H7971), let go to raise himself, grows into the bosh (H954), the open shame, of the very mother who indulged him.

16.text: When the wicked grow many, so does transgression; but the righteous will look upon their downfall.
16.amp: When the wicked [rasha] are multiplied [rabah — become many], transgression [pesha] increases [rabah — the same verb, doubled]; but the righteous [tsaddiq] shall see [raah — look upon] their fall [maphelet — their collapse, their ruin].
16.notes: rabah (H7235) is repeated — as the rasha multiply, so does pesha (H6588); sin breeds in proportion to the sinners. Yet the proverb sets a horizon beyond the present flood: the tsaddiq (H6662) will raah (H7200) the maphelet (H4658), the downfall of the wicked, an assurance that their increase is not the last word.

17.text: Correct your son, and he will give you rest; yes, he will bring delight to your soul.
17.amp: Correct [yasar — discipline, train by chastening] your son [ben], and he will give you rest [nuach — settled quiet, relief]; yes, he will give [natan] delights [maadan — sweet pleasures] to your soul [nephesh].
17.notes: yasar (H3256) is formative discipline, the loving labor of training. Its harvest is the parent's nuach (H5117) — the deep rest of a child turned out well — and maadan (H4574), delicacies for the nephesh (H5315). The verse is the promise behind the rod of v.15: present correction buys future peace.

18.text: Where there is no vision from God, the people throw off all restraint; but blessed is the one who keeps the law.
18.amp: Where there is no vision [chazon — prophetic revelation, a word seen from God], the people [am] cast off restraint [para — run wild, break loose, are let loose like a mob]; but he who keeps [shamar — guards, observes] the law [torah — instruction, teaching], blessed [esher — happy, well-off] is he.
18.notes: chazon (H2377) is the revelatory word of the prophet; without it an am (H5971) does not merely err but para (H6544) — breaks loose, unbridled, as the margin's 'made naked' suggests. The antidote is not unfettered freedom but the torah (H8451) shamar (H8104), the kept word — and there alone is esher (H835), true blessedness.

19.text: A servant is not corrected by words alone; for though he understands, he will not respond.
19.amp: A servant [ebed — a slave, a bondman] will not be corrected [yasar — disciplined, brought to order] by words [dabar] alone; for though he understands [biyn — discerns the meaning], he gives no answer [maaneh — no response, no obedient reply].
19.notes: yasar (H3256) returns from v.17, but here words fail to reform: the hardened ebed (H5650) biyn (H995) — he grasps the command fully — yet withholds the maaneh (H4617), the answering obedience. Knowledge without will to obey is the proverb's portrait of the unteachable heart.

20.text: Do you see a man hasty with his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
20.amp: Do you see [chazah — behold, observe closely] a man [ish] hasty [uts — pressed, rushing, headlong] in his words [dabar]? There is more hope [tikvah — expectation, a cord to hold to] for a fool [kesil] than for him.
20.notes: uts (H213) is to press and hurry — speech that outruns thought. The verdict is startling: the kesil (H3684), the dull fool, has more tikvah (H8615) than the rash talker, because the fool may yet learn what the hasty man's runaway tongue keeps undoing. Words spilled in haste are a deeper folly than slow-witted ignorance.

21.text: Pamper a servant from his youth, and in the end he will turn out ungrateful and grasping.
21.amp: He who delicately rears [panaq — coddles, indulges] his servant [ebed] from childhood [noar — his early youth] will have him become a son [manon — in the end, presuming on the rights of an heir] at the last [acharit — the final outcome].
21.notes: panaq (H6445) is to pamper or treat with soft indulgence. The closing word manon (H4497) is rare and uncertain — traditionally a 'son' who oversteps his place; the sense is that the over-indulged ebed (H5650) ends, in the acharit (H319), presuming on privileges never his. Misplaced softness, like missing discipline (v.15), spoils its object.

22.text: The man given to anger keeps kindling quarrels, and the one whom fury masters piles up transgression upon transgression.
22.amp: A man [ish] of anger [aph — the flaring nostril] kindles [garah — provokes, stirs to contention] quarrels [madon — strife, discord]; and one mastered [baal — owner, lord] by fury [chemah — burning heat, wrath] piles up [rav — has much, abounds in] transgression [pesha].
22.notes: aph (H639) is anger pictured as the flared nostril; chemah (H2534) is the hotter inward boil. The angry man does not merely fall into sin but garah (H1624) madon (H4066), actively breeds quarrels — and where wrath is the master (baal, H1167), pesha (H6588) is not occasional but abundant (rav, H7227).

23.text: A man's pride will bring him low, but the humble in spirit will lay hold of honor.
23.amp: A man's [adam] pride [gaavah — haughtiness, the lifted-up self] shall bring him low [shaphel — humble, cast down]; but honor [kavod — weight, glory] shall uphold [tamak — take firm hold of, sustain] the lowly [shaphal — humble, brought down] in spirit [ruach].
23.notes: the verse turns on a single root sounded two ways: gaavah (H1346), the high self, is made shaphel (H8213), low — while the shaphal (H8217), the already-low in ruach (H7307), is the one kavod (H3519), glory, takes hold of (tamak, H8551). The great reversal of the gospel is already here: the way up is down (cf. Lk 14:11; Jas 4:6).

24.text: Whoever shares with a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse laid down, yet says nothing.
24.amp: Whoever shares as partner [chalaq — divides the spoil] with a thief [gannab] hates [sane] his own soul [nephesh]; he hears [shama — hears, and is bound to obey] the curse [alah — the solemn oath of imprecation], yet does not disclose [nagad — declare, testify to] it.
24.notes: the alah (H423) is the public oath calling down a curse on any who knows of the crime and stays silent. The accomplice who chalaq (H2505) with the gannab (H1590) is caught: to confess implicates himself, to keep quiet falls under the curse — so he sane (H8130) his own nephesh (H5315), trapping his soul to shield a thief.

25.text: The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.
25.amp: The fear [cherdah — dread, anxious trembling] of man [adam] brings [natan] a snare [moqesh]; but whoever trusts [batach — leans his whole weight, rests confident] in the LORD [YHWH] shall be set on high [sagab — lifted to a safe, unreachable height].
25.notes: cherdah (H2731) is the trembling that fears men more than God — a moqesh (H4170) that ensnares the soul into cowardice and compromise. Its cure is batach (H982), trust that leans wholly on YHWH; such a one is sagab (H7682), set so high that danger cannot reach him (the margin: 'set on high'). Two fears, two ends — the dread of man traps, the trust in God lifts.

26.text: Many court the ruler's favor, but it is from the LORD that a man receives justice.
26.amp: Many [rav] seek [baqash] the ruler's [mashal] favor [panim — his face, his good-will]; but a man's [ish] judgment [mishpat — his just due, his verdict] comes from the LORD [YHWH].
26.notes: the idiom is literally to seek the face (panim, H6440) of the one who rules (mashal, H4910) — the courtier's anxious pursuit of human patronage. The proverb relativizes it all: the final mishpat (H4941), what a man truly receives, comes not from the throne men crowd around but from YHWH, the Judge above every judge.

27.text: An unjust man is detestable to the righteous, and the one whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked.
27.amp: An unjust [evel — wicked, perverse in dealing] man [ish] is an abomination [toebah — a detestable, loathsome thing] to the just [tsaddiq]; and he who is upright [yashar] in the way [derek] is an abomination [toebah] to the wicked [rasha].
27.notes: toebah (H8441) is the strongest word of loathing, used of what God Himself abhors. The book ends its collection on this mutual revulsion: the tsaddiq (H6662) and the rasha (H7563) cannot abide each other, for each is to the other what darkness is to light. The two ways set side by side in chapter 1 prove, at the last, to be incompatible.
